How fiber laser tube cutting works A fiber laser tube cutting machine holds the workpiece in rotating chucks and cuts as the section turns beneath a fixed cutting head. Because the machine controls rotation and length together, it can produce cope cuts, saddle joints, holes, slots, and angled end profiles in a single automated pass — geometry that would otherwise take a bandsaw, a drill, and hand grinding to fit up. For a fabrication shop the saving is mostly in what comes after the cut. Sections come off the machine with weld-ready end profiles and pre-cut holes, so assembly is faster and fit-up is consistent from part to part. If you are currently sawing tube and grinding joints by hand, a tube laser usually removes more labour than adding a second sheet cutter would. Tube laser vs. saw and drill Fiber laser tube cutter Bandsaw + drill + manual fit-up End profiles Cope, saddle, miter, angled — cut automatically Hand-ground to fit Holes & slots Cut in the same operation Separate drilling / punching step Fit-up consistency Repeatable to ±0.05mm Varies with the operator Handling One setup, one machine Multiple stations and handoffs Weld prep Comes off the machine ready to assemble Manual grinding before welding What profiles can it cut? Both Wavlon TubeCut platforms handle round tube and square and rectangular HSS. The Double Chuck also cuts custom profiles; the Triple Chuck is built for large round and square structural sections. Common work includes: Round tube — handrail, mechanical tube, hydraulic line, and pipe Square and rectangular HSS — structural framing, trailers, and equipment frames Channel and angle — supports, brackets, and cross-members Large structural sections — heavy round and square profiles on the Triple Chuck Sizing the machine: diameter, length, and power Three numbers decide which platform fits, and they usually matter in this order: Section size. The Double Chuck covers round and square profiles up to 360mm; the Triple Chuck reaches 680mm round and 570mm square. If your largest section fits inside 360mm, the Double Chuck is the natural home. Bed length. The Double Chuck runs a 6,000mm bed; the Triple Chuck a 12,000mm bed. If you cut 12-metre structural steel, bed length settles the choice before anything else does. Laser power. Within a platform, power sets how thick a wall you cut and how fast. The Double Chuck spans 1.5–12kW across four models; the Triple Chuck 6–30kW across three. As with sheet cutting, size to the wall thickness you run regularly rather than the heaviest section you have ever handled. Load weight is the number that gets forgotten. The Double Chuck is rated to 250kg per load; the Triple Chuck to 1,500kg. Long, heavy structural sections can exceed the Double Chuck's limit well before they exceed its diameter capacity — check the weight of your typical stick, not just its size. Why the third chuck matters A double-chuck machine grips the workpiece at two points. A triple-chuck machine adds a middle chuck that supports the section through the cut, which keeps long, heavy profiles from deflecting and holds accuracy where a two-chuck setup would start to sag. That is why the Triple Chuck is the platform for 12-metre beds and 1,500kg loads — the extra support, not just the extra power, is what makes heavy structural work repeatable. title: BLT Laser Head Technology Features | Wavlon Lasers
description: 23 intelligent features built into BOCI BLT laser cutting heads — optical precision, protection systems, and cutting intelligence. Every feature explained for fabricators.
text: Home / Technologies / Laser Cutting Head / Technology Features BOCI BLT · Intelligent Technology BLT Laser Head Technology Features Every BLT head ships with a suite of intelligent sensors, monitoring systems, and cutting algorithms. Here's what each one does — and why it matters on the shop floor. 23 + Intelligent Features 3 groups Function Categories 6 series Head Models Overview Technology Features Selection Guide Model Specs Group 1 of 3 Optical & Precision The features that control beam delivery, focus accuracy, and position stability. These directly determine cut edge quality and how consistently the head performs over long production runs. Why optical precision matters on the shop floor A 0.1mm focus drift is invisible to the eye but produces inconsistent kerf width, increased dross, and failed edge tolerances on tight-profile parts. Every feature in this group exists to keep the beam exactly where the CNC program says it should be — automatically, without operator intervention. See which head has which features → Less Focusing Time Fast Focusing Focal position is adjusted by moving the collimating lens rather than the focusing lens. This delivers faster focus travel speed (up to 500 mm/s) and eliminates mechanical hysteresis in the focusing path — reducing setup time between material thicknesses. Higher Cutting Precision Built-In Capacitance Amplifier The capacitance sensor that measures nozzle-to-workpiece distance is amplified on-board the head itself — not in a remote controller box. This reduces electrical noise in the signal, giving the Z-axis servo a cleaner input and resulting in more precise height following on warped or uneven plate. More Stable Cutting Focusing Lens Monitoring A thermal sensor continuously monitors the temperature of the focusing lens during operation. If the lens becomes contaminated and begins absorbing laser energy, the temperature rises above threshold — the system automatically stops the laser and raises an alarm before the lens fractures or the cut quality degrades enough to scrap a part. Intelligent Cutting Real-Time Focus Centering A camera collects molten pool images during cutting. The sensor detects any coaxial deviation between the laser beam axis and the nozzle center, then automatically adjusts in real time. This ensures the beam stays centered in the kerf even as the head warms up or components drift — critical for consistent edge quality over long production runs. Simpler Centering Quick Focus Centering Traditional nozzle centering uses tape and burn marks — slow, subjective, and operator-dependent. Quick Focus Centering replaces this with one-click visual centering through the head's built-in camera. Nozzle replacement takes seconds instead of minutes, reducing production interruptions during shift changeovers. Efficient Cutting Variable Beam Shape Available on BLT-9MA series (30–60kW). Switches between M1 small spot mode (concentrated energy — high speed on thin sheet) and M2 large spot mode (distributed energy — deep penetration on ultra-thick plate) within the same head. Eliminates the need to swap heads when moving between thin-sheet and heavy-plate work on the same machine shift. Group 2 of 3 Protection & Monitoring Nine systems that watch over the head's optical components, gas delivery, and production environment — and take automatic corrective action before problems become downtime or scrapped parts. Smart and More Efficient Closed-Loop Monitoring Multiple sensors feed real-time status data back to the cutting controller in a closed loop. The system continuously cross-references actual cutting conditions against expected parameters — automatically diagnosing deviations and raising early warnings before they become failures. This is the foundation that all other monitoring features build on. More Stable Cutting Full-Body Water Cooling A water-cooling circuit covers 90% of the cutting head's optical path — including the collimating lens, focusing lens, and body. Optical components held at a stable temperature maintain their alignment and coating integrity over long production runs, especially at higher power levels where heat generation is significant. More Stable Cutting Nozzle Cooling A dedicated cooling circuit inside the nozzle section keeps the nozzle tip temperature stable during continuous cutting. Nozzle degradation from heat is one of the most common causes of inconsistent cut edge quality — especially on long uninterrupted cuts. This extends nozzle service life and widens the operating window for batch production. Longer Windows Lifespan 3 / 4 Sets of Protective Windows The protective window sits below the focusing lens and takes the direct hit from spatter and back-reflections. Higher-series heads include 3 or 4 separate protective windows in the optical stack — each additional window extends the service interval before the focusing lens itself is exposed, dramatically reducing the cost of lens replacement. More Stable Cutting Protective Window Monitoring A temperature sensor monitors the protective window in real time during operation. When contamination causes the window to begin absorbing laser energy, its temperature rises — the system automatically stops the laser and sounds an alarm before the window shatters. This prevents lens contamination and eliminates unplanned downtime from window failure mid-cut. More Stable Cutting Cutting Gas Pressure Monitoring The assist gas pressure at the nozzle tip is monitored in real time. Gas supply interruptions, pressure drops, or line restrictions are detected immediately — the system alerts the operator before gas loss causes dross formation, incomplete cuts, or oxidation on stainless steel. Particularly important for nitrogen-assist cutting where gas pressure directly determines edge finish quality. Protect the Protective Windows Bottom Protective Cartridge Sealing Monitors the integrity of the sealing around the protective window cartridge. A failed seal allows cutting debris and vapour to enter the optical cavity — causing progressive contamination that the operator can't see until cut quality has already degraded. This sensor catches seal failures before they cause optical damage. Safer Production Protective Window Anti-Explosion An upgraded contamination detection algorithm monitors stray light from the protective window continuously. When a window approaches failure, stray light patterns change in characteristic ways — the system detects this before the window fractures and shuts down the laser safely. Prevents the dangerous and expensive scenario of a shattered window inside the cutting head during production. Easy Troubleshooting Stray Light Monitoring Stray light — laser energy scattered outside the intended beam path — causes thermal damage to the head's internal components and can indicate a developing problem with the optical alignment or a contaminated lens. This sensor detects stray light in real time, triggers an alarm, and helps operators identify the source of the problem before it causes equipment damage or a safety incident. Group 3 of 3 Cutting Intelligence Process automation features that reduce operator dependency, improve throughput, and prevent scrapped parts — from smart piercing decisions to collision recovery. Automation that keeps the machine running A laser cutting machine's throughput is limited by its weakest link — and in most shops, that's operator attention. Smart piercing, auto recut, and co-edge monitoring let the machine make real-time decisions that would otherwise require the operator to be watching every cut. The result is higher utilization with fewer people on the floor. Smart Piercing · Auto Recut · Smart Laser Off Simpler Maintenance Collision Protection A break-away mechanical mount absorbs impact when the head collides with raised workpiece edges, remnant scrap, or clamps. Protective screws allow the head to deflect rather than transmit the impact force to the optical components. The head realigns to its zero position automatically — no depot repair, no realignment procedure, no downtime. The operator resets and continues cutting. Enhance Piercing Efficiency Smart Piercing Traditional piercing uses fixed timed parameters — the laser pulses for a set duration regardless of whether the material has actually pierced. Smart Piercing monitors the piercing process in real time using backscatter detection and immediately advances to the cutting move the moment the pierce is confirmed. This reduces average pierce time, prevents over-piercing damage on thin material, and eliminates the most common source of part-start defects. Stable and Efficient Cutting Auto Recut (Process Monitoring) The head monitors the cutting kerf using a sensor. If a section of a part is detected as not fully cut through — due to a focus drift, gas interruption, or material inconsistency — the cutting head automatically returns to the failed section and re-cuts it. This prevents incomplete parts reaching the next production stage and eliminates the need for manual part inspection after every cut. Improve Cutting Quality Smart Laser Off Controls the exact moment the laser shuts off relative to head movement at the end of a contour. Imprecise laser-off timing leaves a characteristic groove or burn mark at the cut exit point — visible on the finished part's edge. Smart Laser Off calculates the optimal shutdown point based on material, power, and speed to produce a clean, slag-free edge at both contour entry and exit. Efficient Cutting Co-Edge Piercing Monitoring When nesting parts, contours that share an edge ("co-edge" or "common line cutting") present a decision point: does the head pierce again at the shared edge, or is a pierce unnecessary because the kerf from the adjacent cut already exists? Co-Edge Piercing Monitoring detects this situation and makes the correct decision automatically — eliminating unnecessary piercing delays and preventing double-piercing damage on thin material. More Stable Cutting Cutting Path Monitoring A sensor monitors the actual kerf width in real time during the cutting pass. If the kerf begins to narrow or widen — indicating a focus drift or process drift — the system intelligently adjusts the focus position to compensate and maintain consistent kerf geometry. This is what enables consistent cutting results across a full 3015 or 4020 sheet without manual re-zeroing during the job. One Time Forming Bevel Cutting Available on BLT-4P series with the AB swing axis. Supports V-bevel, Y-bevel, and X-bevel profiles up to ±45° in a single pass — no secondary beveling operation needed. Used for weld-prep on structural steel and pressure vessel components. The swing axis compensates for head tilt to maintain consistent nozzle standoff and gas assist angle during the bevel pass. Wide Application 3D Sensing Head Available on BLT-3T, BLT-4T, and BLT-5H tube cutting heads. The 3D sensing head adapts to the complex geometry of structural profiles — round tubes, square tubes, I-beams, C-channels, angle iron, and custom profiles. Its compact interference area fits into the tight spaces between tube flanges and web sections, enabling cuts that conventional heads cannot reach. Quick Reference Which features come with which heads? Not every feature is available on every BLT model. Higher series heads include more monitoring and intelligence. On this page Choosing laser power Sheet cutting or tube cutting What's different about buying in Canada The Wavlon range at a glance Cost, financing, and payback What support should include A fiber laser cutter is usually the largest single capital purchase a fabrication shop makes. The specification decisions you make up front — power, bed size, enclosure, automation — determine what work you can quote for the next decade. This guide covers the choices that matter most, and the ones that are easy to get wrong. 1. Choosing laser power Laser power is the first number everyone asks about, and the most common place to overspend. Higher wattage does two things: it raises the maximum thickness you can cut, and it cuts thin material faster. If your work is mostly thin gauge, extra kilowatts buy you speed rather than capability — and speed only pays if you have the order book to keep the machine loaded. A practical way to size the machine: take the thickest material you cut regularly , not the thickest you have ever cut. One-off thick jobs are usually cheaper to outsource than to buy capacity for. If you mostly cut Look at Power Configuration question Varied sheet work with open loading access ProCut Series 3–12kW How will sheets be loaded and the cutting area guarded? Production runs where enclosure and safety matter PowerCut Series 3–12kW Does the cabin and loading layout suit your floor plan? Sheet production with repeated loading cycles UltraCut Series 3–20kW+ Can preparing the next sheet reduce your current loading delays? Qualify the cut, not just the maximum thickness. Request a review of representative parts at your everyday thickness. Confirm the material grade, assist gas, edge finish and cutting conditions for the proposed configuration. 2. Sheet cutting or tube cutting These are different machines, not settings on the same machine. A flat-bed sheet cutter works on plate held on a slatted bed. A tube cutter holds the workpiece in rotating chucks and cuts as it turns, which is what allows cope cuts, saddle joints, and angled end profiles on structural sections. If you are currently bandsawing tube and then grinding fit-up by hand, a tube laser usually removes more labour than a second sheet machine would. Weld prep that used to be a manual operation comes off the machine ready to assemble. Choosing between the two tube platforms TubeCut Double Chuck — 1.5–12kW, sections to 360mm, 6,000mm bed. Two synchronized chucks. The practical entry point for most shops. TubeCut Triple Chuck — 6–30kW, sections to 680mm round, 12,000mm bed, loads to 1,500kg. The third chuck supports the workpiece through the cut, which is what holds accuracy on long, heavy structural profiles. The deciding factor is usually section size and length rather than power. If you are running 12-metre structural steel, bed length settles the question before wattage does. 3. What's different about buying in Canada Most fiber laser specifications are written for other markets. Three things reliably catch Canadian buyers out: Electrical supply Canadian industrial shops commonly run 600V three-phase, while many machines arrive configured for other standards. This has to be sorted before the machine ships, not discovered on installation day. Confirm the proposed electrical configuration and applicable safety requirements in writing, with your electrician involved before delivery. Currency and financing A machine quoted in US dollars exposes you to exchange-rate movement between quote and delivery — a real cost on a purchase this size, and one that is rarely mentioned in the sales conversation. Confirm the quote currency, payment schedule and any currency-adjustment terms before committing. Who actually shows up This is the one that matters most and is hardest to verify before you buy. Ask directly: who performs the installation, where is the technician based, and what is the response commitment when the machine is down? A machine that is cheaper up front but waits weeks for an overseas technician is not cheaper. A useful question to ask any supplier: "If this machine stops on a Tuesday morning, what happens, and who do I call?" The specificity of the answer tells you most of what you need to know. 4. Cost, financing, and payback Purchase price is only part of the operating picture. When you compare quotes, account for assist gas consumption, consumables such as nozzles and protective windows, electrical supply work, and whether the machine needs a water chiller and the plumbing to serve it. If you are considering financing, request the current lender terms, eligibility requirements, payment schedule and total cost for your proposed purchase. Availability and approval depend on the provider and applicant. Confirm which purchase and installation costs are included in the financing proposal. See financing options → 6. What support should include Support is the part of the purchase that is easiest to promise and hardest to check. As a baseline, a Canadian buyer should expect all four of the following in writing: On-site installation and commissioning — confirm responsibilities for rigging, levelling, alignment, calibration and first-part testing, with agreed acceptance criteria. Operator training at your facility — confirm the scope, location, duration and cost of training in machine operation, software, nesting, maintenance and safety. Warranty scope — request the duration, covered components, labour coverage, exclusions and claim process for the configuration being quoted. Remote diagnostics — confirm available remote troubleshooting, access requirements and when an on-site visit may be needed. text: Home / Blog / Dual Exchange Tables / How Dual Exchange Tables Work How Dual Exchange Tables Improve Fiber Laser Workflow Two tables let cutting and material preparation share the same production window. October 4, 2026 · By Wavlon Lasers A fast cutting process is only part of a productive sheet metal operation. Between sheets, someone still needs to remove finished parts, clear the skeleton, bring in new material, and prepare the next job. A dual exchange table lets a shop overlap some of that work with cutting. The Wavlon UltraCut Series combines an enclosed cutting cabin with two exchange tables. One table is in the cutting position while the second is available for material handling at the external loading position. Watch the UltraCut video ▶ Play UltraCut video Play to load YouTube. Watch on YouTube How the dual exchange cycle works Cut the first sheet. The laser processes the sheet inside the enclosed cabin. Prepare the external table. Following the machine's operating procedures, remove completed parts and the remaining skeleton, then load the next sheet. Exchange the tables. Once cutting is complete and the machine is ready, the tables exchange positions. Begin the next job. Cutting resumes on the prepared sheet while the completed sheet becomes accessible for unloading. The advantage is the overlap: material handling can happen during the cutting cycle instead of all of it being added after the cut. The loading area still needs clear access, suitable lifting equipment, and a trained operator. Single table or dual exchange tables? Consideration Single table Dual exchange tables Sheet changeover Loading and unloading generally use the same table as cutting. External handling can overlap with cutting on the other table. Production pattern Worth considering for intermittent work and lower sheet volumes. Worth considering for repeated sheet processing and sustained production. Floor planning Plan for the machine and material access. Also allow for table travel, loading access, and clearance. Output constraint Handling time adds to time between cutting jobs. Handling can still delay the next cycle if the external table is not ready. Where the time savings come from Consider an illustrative job with eight minutes of cutting and four minutes of unloading and loading. With sequential handling, those activities take twelve minutes before allowing for other setup steps. If handling can be completed during the eight-minute cut on a dual-table system, the repeating cycle can approach eight minutes plus the table exchange and any remaining checks. This is a workflow example, not an UltraCut performance claim. Actual results depend on the nest, material, thickness, power, handling equipment, operator readiness, exchange time, and job setup. If cutting finishes before unloading and loading are complete, the machine may still wait. Measuring both cutting and handling time on representative jobs is more useful than assuming that a second table will eliminate every pause. When should a shop consider dual exchange tables? Repeated sheet changeovers: production involves enough sheets for handling time to become a recurring constraint. Available material handling: operators and lifting equipment can prepare the second table during the cut. A suitable shop layout: the exchange area, sheet storage, scrap removal, and finished-part staging can remain accessible. A balanced downstream process: sorting, bending, and other operations can keep up with the planned laser output. Choosing an UltraCut configuration UltraCut offers standard 3–20 kW configurations and 3015 or 4020 frame options. Choose the cutting power and working area around your material mix, sheet sizes, edge requirements, and expected workload. Table configuration alone does not determine cutting speed or part quality. Review the UltraCut specifications , explore the sheet cutting guide , and discuss installation and operator training with our Canadian service team . Questions to bring to your machine review How long do cutting and material handling each take on your typical nests? What sheet sizes, materials, and thicknesses will you process? How will you lift sheets, unload parts, and remove skeletons? Where will the machine, moving tables, and material staging fit? Which source, cutting head, controls, training, and support are included in the quotation? Send Wavlon your production requirements to review an UltraCut configuration for your shop. Explore more in Dual Exchange Tables or return to the Wavlon Blog . Planning a Canadian installation? Review our regional guide for Ontario, Montréal, Vancouver, and Calgary and quote-comparison checklist before choosing the machine and delivery scope. Answers for your buying decision When is a dual exchange table worth the extra cost? A dual exchange table is worth evaluating when repeated loading and unloading cause the laser to wait between sheets. It allows some material handling to overlap with cutting, provided the external table is ready on time. Compare the complete cycle on representative nests and include floor space, lifting equipment, staffing and downstream capacity in the decision. If your bottleneck is programming, deburring or bending, an extra table may not solve it. Review UltraCut against your actual production sequence.

text: Home / Education Center / Nitrogen vs Oxygen vs Air for Fiber Laser Cutting Nitrogen vs Oxygen vs Air for Fiber Laser Cutting Compare nitrogen, oxygen and compressed air for fiber laser cutting. Understand edge requirements, gas supply and the checks to include in a cutting trial. By Wavlon Lasers · Published October 10, 2026 Quick answer Choose assist gas around the material and the edge required for the next operation. Nitrogen supports fusion cutting, oxygen contributes to a reactive cutting process, and compressed air requires a compatible machine setup and an acceptable tested edge. Precitec ProCutter Thunder cutting head. Confirm the configuration for your application. In this guide What assist gas does Compare the gas options Start with the next manufacturing operation Include the complete gas supply Compare gas options on the same job What assist gas does Assist gas helps remove molten material from the cut. The choice also changes the process at the edge. In nitrogen fusion cutting, the laser supplies the cutting energy while the gas clears the melt and helps protect the edge from surrounding air. Oxygen reacts with the metal and contributes energy during flame cutting. These are different processes, so a gas change is not simply a purchasing substitution. TRUMPF explains the underlying mechanisms in its references on fusion cutting and flame cutting . Those general principles do not establish settings or performance for a particular Wavlon configuration. Compare the gas options Assist gas selection questions Option Process consideration Question for the trial Nitrogen Often selected where limiting edge oxidation is important. Does the finished edge meet the appearance and next-operation requirements? Oxygen Reactive cutting adds heat and can leave an oxidized edge. What edge preparation does the coating or welding process require? Compressed air Contains oxygen; requires suitable treatment, delivery and an approved cutting process. Is the tested edge acceptable, and what air quality and supply equipment are required? This table is a selection aid, not a parameter chart. Do not transfer nozzle sizes, pressure values or focus settings from another machine. Use the process approved for the installed cutting head, laser source and machine. Start with the next manufacturing operation A visually clean cut is only one part of acceptance. Bring the coating, welding, assembly or inspection requirement into the cutting trial. A part that looks acceptable at the table may still need preparation before its next operation. For painted parts, ask the coating provider what edge preparation is required. For welded assemblies, have the responsible welding team assess the cut edge against the applicable procedure. For exposed components, agree on appearance criteria using an actual sample. The supplier should know which requirement the trial is intended to demonstrate. Avoid assuming that one gas eliminates all finishing. Burr, geometry, surface condition and the drawing can create additional requirements even when oxidation is well controlled. Include the complete gas supply Ask the equipment supplier and gas provider to agree on purity, quality, flow and delivery requirements at the machine inlet. A supply specification should identify the operating conditions, not only the name of the gas. Confirm what is included in the machine quotation and what belongs to the site installation. For nitrogen, compare the proposed supply arrangement against expected usage and delivery logistics. For compressed air, include the compressor, drying, filtration, storage and maintenance requirements specified for the process. Existing shop air should not be assumed suitable simply because it is already available. Record supplier assumptions about continuous operation and peak demand. If several machines share the supply, ask how simultaneous operation will be supported. Have qualified providers determine the installation details. Compare gas options on the same job Use one representative nest and agree on the same acceptance criteria for each permitted gas option. Record the material grade and thickness, elapsed cutting time, gas consumption where measured, quantity of acceptable parts, and finishing time. Keep setup changes with the result. Compare the complete outcome: a faster cut may not be the best choice if the next operation needs extra work. Similarly, an option with a lower gas purchase cost may require additional supply equipment or maintenance. Ask suppliers to show their assumptions rather than accepting a single cost-per-part claim. Send the drawing and intended finish when requesting a Wavlon application review . Pair the gas discussion with our laser power selection guide and the current cutting-head options . Frequently asked questions Is compressed air a direct replacement for nitrogen? No. Air contains oxygen and needs an approved process, suitable treatment and a compatible supply system. Validate the resulting edge against the part requirements before selecting it. Does nitrogen cutting mean that no finishing is needed? Not necessarily. Inspect burr, dimensions, appearance and the requirements of the next operation. An edge with limited oxidation may still need other preparation. Nitrogen is commonly used where an oxide-free edge is important; oxygen supports an oxidation-assisted cutting process; compressed air can be an option on compatible configurations when its edge result is acceptable. Validate the complete process rather than choosing on gas price alone. Confirm gas quality, supply capacity and machine requirements with the supplier. Compare finishing and downstream welding or coating as well as cutting speed. Do not transfer gas settings from a different machine.

Ask for a nesting and cutting review using your own parts, with the remaining unusable stock stated explicitly. Compare both processes on the same material, thickness, drawings and finished-part acceptance criteria. Laser is worth evaluating for fine features and demanding tolerances; plasma is worth evaluating where its cut quality meets the job and its equipment and running costs suit the workload. Avoid double-counting costs already included in a supplier price or an ownership estimate. Treat raw-material differences, scrap credits and financing separately and document your assumptions. Check the capacity behind the estimate A machine’s available shift hours are not all productive hours. Account for programming, loading, sorting, planned maintenance and interruptions. A cutting trial helps estimate the work cycle; it does not establish future demand. Simple payback omits the timing of cash flows, financing, tax effects and residual value. Use it as an initial comparison and review a fuller cash-flow model before committing funds. Build the installed and operating budget and prepare a comparable quotation . Answers for your buying decision When does buying a laser make more sense than outsourcing? Buying deserves a closer look when repeat work, outside cutting spend and delivery constraints can support the full cost of ownership at realistic utilization. Outsourcing may remain a better fit for occasional work, uncertain demand, specialist materials or a shop without the staff and floor space to run the process. A mixed approach can keep unusual or overflow jobs with suppliers. Compare the same part mix and quality requirements. Include programming, material handling, secondary finishing, rejected parts, maintenance and downtime as well as the machine payment. Validate demand before treating unused capacity as future revenue. How should I estimate payback without assuming full utilization? Estimate simple payback using the installed investment divided by positive annual net cash savings. Build those savings from work you can realistically bring in-house, after operating costs and continuing outside work. Test low, expected and higher demand cases, allowing for setup, maintenance, staffing gaps and rejected parts. If annual net savings are zero or negative, that scenario has no simple payback. Keep the investment and savings on the same basis: do not subtract loan principal in annual savings and also count the full machine price as the investment. Review financing, tax and cash-flow effects separately with your adviser.
